Tentative Rulings
March 19, 2026
Judge Joseph Ortiz

Tentative Rulings for Department S-17 are posted on the court’s website (https://www.sb-
court.org/divisions/civil/civil-tentative-rulings) at 3:00 p.m. or at 7:00 p.m. the court day before
the hearing. If no tentative ruling is posted at 3:00 p.m., please check again after 7:00 p.m.
Unless you wish to submit on the tentative ruling, you must appear for the hearing either in
person, CourtCall (888-882-6878 or www.courtcall.com), or by ZOOM. Failure to appear is
deemed a waiver of oral argument. If you wish to submit to the tentative, please call the
Judicial Assistant at (909) 708-8715 in advance of the hearing. If all parties submit on a
tentative ruling, it will become final. The tentative ruling may seek input on particular issues
and direct appearance. If so directed, attendance at the hearing is mandatory. The party
prevailing on a motion or other hearing shall serve written notice of the court’s ruling unless all
parties waive notice of the ruling.

ATTENTION: Since January 9, 2023, the court no longer provides an official Court Reporter to
transcribe proceedings. Parties who wish to have a transcript must retain their own private
reporter and must submit a “Stipulation and Order to Use Certified Shorthand Reporter.”
Parties who do not retain their own reporter have waived the right to one.
UNLESS OTHERWISE NOTED, THE PREVAILING PARTY IS TO GIVE NOTICE OF THE RULING.
16. Lopez v. United Parcel Service, Inc., et al, Case No. CIVSB2512060
Defendant UPS’s Motion for Judgment on the Pleadings
3/19/26, 9:00 a.m., Dept. S-17
The Court would CONTINUE the matter so that movant may satisfy the meet-and-confer
requirements.

Prior to a Motion for Judgment on the Pleadings, a party is required meet and confer in person
or by telephone or by video conference. (Code Civ. Proc., § 439(a) [JOP].)
Here, the supporting declaration does not confirm compliance with the meet-and-confer
requirements. (See Ebsworth Decl.) Rather, the declaration indicates only that emails went back
and forth between the parties and that an offer for a phone call was made. (Ibid.) Defendant
will file a supplemental declaration, showing satisfaction of the requirements, at least five days
before the next hearing with a courtesy copy lodged directly in the department.
*** *** ***
17. Khadka v. K-Towne 88, et al, Case No. CIVSB2408413
Plaintiff’s Motion to Deem Requests for Admission, Set One, as Admitted
3/19/26, 9:00 a.m., Dept. S-17
Tentative Rulings
The Court would GRANT this unopposed motion. The Court would also grant sanctions in the
amount of $585, payable within thirty days.

Case Summary
This is a business dispute. Plaintiff alleges that on November 6, 2023, he entered into a written
agreement to purchase a business, namely K-Towne 88. Defendant Carabatsos was the seller.
In essence, Plaintiff alleges that Defendant Carabatsos breached by selling to a third-party and
refusing to return Plaintiff’s down payment. As such, he filed suit on March 13, 2024, alleging
(1) fraud; (2) intentional misrepresentation; (3) negligent misrepresentation; (4) breach of
contract; and (5) conversion.

Analysis
As a preliminary matter, Defendant Carabatsos’s opposition may not be considered given that
he does not have any standing. Defendant K-Towne 88 is a separate entity, even if now a
dissolved corporation. Further Carabatsos’s opposition is directed to arguments that discovery
was not properly served on Carabatsos and that he has responded to the Requests for
Admission. Such arguments are irrelevant where the motion is directed to K-Towne 88 and not
Carabatsos.

Further, Defendant K-Towne 88 is unrepresented and, in general, a corporation, whether
dissolved or not, may not appear in an action pro per. “In California, a corporation may not
represent itself, except in a small claims proceeding.” (Gamat v. Blanchard (2001) 91
Cal.App.4th 1276, 1284, FN5.) It is the duty of the trial judge to advise the representative of the
corporation of the necessity to be represented by an attorney. (Ibid.)
In support of the motion, Plaintiff’s counsel states that on July 23, 2025, her office served
Defendant K-Towne 88 with Plaintiff’s Requests for Admissions, Set One, by mail. No verified or
unverified responses have been received. (Sabarwal Decl., ¶¶2-3.) Plaintiff’s counsel does not
attach a copy of the proof of service that shows service of the RFAs on Defendant K-Towne 88:
thus, the Court only has Plaintiff’s counsel statement in support of service of the RFAs.
However, given that Plaintiff’s counsel attests to service of the RFAs under penalty of perjury
and there is no opposition, the Court would grant the motion the unopposed motion.
*** *** ***
18. Williams v. Advantage Care Facility, Inc., et al, Case No. CIVSB2527611
Defendant A Life Hospice’s Demurrer
3/19/26, 9:00 a.m., Dept. S-17
Tentative Ruling
The Court would SUSTAIN the demurrer as to the first and fourth causes of action with thirty
days leave to amend. The Court would OVERRULE the demurrer as to the second cause.
Case Summary
This is, in essence, an elder abuse case. Plaintiff alleges that she is the surviving daughter of the
decedent. Decedent passed on October 4, 2024. Around March 15, 2023, Plaintiff alleges that
decedent signed an admissions agreement with Defendant Advantage for lodging, meals, and
services. He also underwent a resident appraisal, which reported that he was visually impaired,
could not stand on his own, lacked coordination, and had muscle weakness. He is alleged to
have suffered a series of medical injuries, including a failed neck surgery that rendered him
paraplegic.

After his admission, Plaintiff alleges there were unauthorized or improper purchases made on
decedent’s Amazon account, which Plaintiff asserts was done by Defendant Advantage. Plaintiff
alleges they were a result of undue influence or coercion. Purchases are alleged to include
camera equipment, magnets, Season 3 of Buffy the Vampire Slayer, cooking machines, screen
protectors, and the like. In addition, there were unauthorized charges to decedent’s bank
account for T-Mobile, despite the fact that decedent had a Verizon account. Charges from July
2023 until his death totaled over two thousand dollars. Plaintiff also asserts that there were
improper rent increases, in violation of the agreement, where Defendant Advantage doubled
decedent’s rent. There were personal checks to Defendant Torres also totaling over two
thousand dollars.

As such, Plaintiff filed suit on September 22, 2025, alleging causes of action for (1) financial
abuse under the Elder Abuse & Dependent Adult Civil Protection Act; (2) negligence; (3) breach
of contract; and (4) violation of the unfair competition law.
Analysis
Here, Defendant A Life Hospice demurs to the causes of action on the grounds that the
Complaint fails to include facts alleging any actions or omission by A Life Hospice that caused
injury, constituted abuse, or violated any statute as to decedent. Rather, Defendant asserts the
Complaint please mere conclusions and grounds all Defendants together for the purpose of
pleading.

Financial Elder Abuse (1st Cause): A claim for financial elder abuse requires (1) that the
defendant took, hid, appropriated, obtained, or retained the plaintiff’s property or assisted in
such; (2) that the plaintiff was 65 years or older or dependent adult at the time of the conduct;
(3) that the defendant took, hid, appropriated, obtained, or retained or assisted in such for
wrongful use or with intent to defraud or by undue influence; (4) that the plaintiff was harmed;
and (5) that the defendant’s conduct was a substantial factor in causing plaintiff’s harm. (CACI
3100.) Certainly, there is a knowledge component such that the offending party either knew or
should have known its conduct is likely to be harmful to the elder person. (Welf. & Inst. Code,
§ 15610.30(b).)
Defendant A Life Hospice argues it provides supportive care only and does not oversee or
control residential care facilities or handle patient finances. The Hospice argues the allegations
of financial elder abuse in the Complaint are directed at Defendants Advantage and Torres, with
nothing specifically linking it to this alleged misconduct. The Hospice claims the Complaint does
not include allegations it accessed financial information, handled money or withdrawals,
retained property, or assisting in taking any asset. Instead, A Life Hospice argues the Complaint
only includes conclusory allegations against it.
Plaintiff argues that Defendant A Life Hospice committed financial elder abuse by knowingly
assisting the co-Defendants abuse. (Compl., ¶82.) Plaintiff argues it can rely on the allegations
made as to Defendants Advantage and Torres because she is claiming Defendants acted in a
coordinated course of conduct and where it is alleged they have acted in concert, collective
pleading suffices. Except, the Complaint does not allege A Life Hospice was acting in concert
with its co-Defendants nor does it allege there was a conspiracy. There is an allegation that
each defendant is an agent of each other but not one asserting that they were acting in concert.
Furthermore, the agency allegation pleads only a legal conclusion with no facts. (See, e.g.,
Compl., ¶ 19.) Furthermore, there is no allegation that A Life Hospice knew or should have
known of the purported financial abuse or that it was harmful, both of which are required
elements. Thus, the Court would sustain.

Negligence (2nd Cause): “The elements of any negligence cause of action are duty, breach of
duty, proximate cause, and damages.” (Peredia v. HR Mobile Services, Inc. (2018) 25 Cal.App.5th
680, 687.)
A Life Hospice argues the Complaint fails to make allegations as to its duty and only includes
legal conclusions to assert that it knew or should have known of the financial abuse. A Life
Hospice argues the allegations fall short even for a claim of negligence. Defendant cites
Bockrath v. Aldrich for the proposition that when “the pleaded facts of negligence and injury do
not naturally give rise to an inference of causation[,] the plaintiff must plead specific facts
affording an inference the one caused the others.” (Bockrath v. Aldrich Chemical Co., Inc. (1999)
21 Cal.4th 71, 79.) In other words, the plaintiff must allege facts explaining how the conduct
caused or contributed to the injury. (Id. at p. 78.)
Notably, however, negligence can be generally pleaded: “A plaintiff need only allege negligence
in general terms, which means that it is sufficient to allege that an act was negligently done
without stating the particular omission which rendered it negligent.” (McBride v. Atchison,
Topeka & Santa Fe Railway Co. (1955) 44 Cal.2d 113, 119.)
Here, the Complaint alleges t a duty of care was breach because the Defendants failed to
protect decedent’s financial matters by accessing or allowing others to access his bank account
and Amazon account. (Compl., ¶¶90-91.) This breach of duty was a direct and proximate cause
of decedent’s injuries for which he suffered damages. (Compl., ¶¶95, 97.) There are also
additional allegations regarding a duty to use reasonable care to ensure decedent’s economic
safety and to supervisor employees in the provision of a safe environment. (Compl., ¶100.)
Finally, the Bockrath case is distinguishable because here the negligence and injury do naturally
give rise to an inference of causation. Thus, the Court would overrule.
Unfair Competition Law (4th Cause): Here, to the extent this claim is predicated on the financial
elder abuse cause, as discussed supra, it fails. To the extent it is predicated on violations of
other statutes, it is not stated how Defendant A Life Hospice violated those other statutes. A
claim for violation of the unfair competition law must plead with reasonable particularity the
facts that support the statutory elements of the violation. (Khoury v. Maly’s of Calif., Inc. (1993)
14 Cal.App.4th 612, 619.) Thus, the Court would sustain.
*** *** ***
20. North Mills Equip. Finance LLC v. Taomore Supply Chain LTD, et al, Case No. CIVSB2400967
Plaintiff’s Motion to Strike Defendants’ Answers
3/19/26, 9:00 a.m., Dept. S-17
The Court would GRANT this unopposed motion and strike the Defendants’ answers. The
motion was made on the grounds that Defendants Taomore Supply and Dong (Defendants)
have failed to comply to the prior Court Order compelling answers to Form Interrogatories and
Special Interrogatories and the payment of sanctions of $1,080. (See Final Ruling, Sept. 9,
2025.) Responses were due within thirty days; yet, as of the date of the motion no responses
were provided. (McKendrick Decl., ¶¶6-7.) Further, no opposition was provided; thus, the Court
is unaware if any subsequent responses having been provided.
*** *** ***
